notes.shape: The yield curve displays yields across Treasury maturities from 1 month to 30 years, with a normal upward slope indicating higher yields for longer maturities. An inverted yield curve, where short-term yields exceed long-term yields, has historically preceded US recessions by 6 to 18 months. Currently, the 10-year Treasury yield stands at 4.71% for June 2026, with the 10-year minus 2-year spread (2s10s) at 0.36 percentage points, indicating a positive slope. This contrasts with the 2022-2024 period when the curve was inverted and the 2s10s spread fell to zero, the deepest inversion in the series.
notes.signal: The 2s10s spread is monitored as a recession indicator because inversion has reliably foreshadowed economic downturns. Although deeply inverted through 2022-2024, the spread has re-steepened above zero to 0.36 points, suggesting reduced recession risk. The New York Fed recession probability currently reads 31%, reflecting a moderate risk assessment. However, the yield curve often un-inverts shortly before a recession, so the absence of inversion does not preclude a forthcoming downturn.
notes.now: At present, the yield curve's upward slope and positive 2s10s spread suggest easing recession concerns relative to the recent inverted period. Nonetheless, a 31% recession probability signals that risks remain notable. The data indicate caution but no immediate recession signal from the yield curve shape alone.
